 Nvidia RTX 3090 performance nearly doubles with free GPU unlock, but there's a catch
 ⓘ Vaidyanathan Subhramaniam, Notebookcheck The RTX 3090 still has some hidden potential six years after launch A new open-source tool reportedly unlocks previously restricted Tensor Core performance on Nvidia's ageing RTX 30-series GPUs, delivering gains of up to 80% in certain compute benchmarks. The modification works without flashing the GPU's VBIOS, although gaming improvements remain unproven. Anil Ganti , Published 10/24/2026 GPU AI 
 4 Reviews     ← exclude selected types     ← exclude selected tags 
 Nvidia’s six-year-old GeForce RTX 3090 apparently has some untapped computing potential. A new open-source project called gpu-unlock, developed by GitHub user Zagitta , can reportedly deliver double-digit improvements in certain Tensor Core workloads without requiring hardware modifications or a patched Nvidia driver. 
 The project targets an instruction-issue rate limitation affecting FP16 and BF16 Tensor Core operations with FP32 accumulation on Ampere-based GeForce cards. According to the developer, the affected operations can run at roughly half the rate available on professional Nvidia GPUs. The unlock changes hardware speed-selection registers to remove that restriction. 
 Interestingly, the technique builds upon earlier research used to unlock capabilities on Nvidia CMP mining GPUs. Zagitta’s implementation uses a Linux kernel module that executes before Nvidia’s graphics driver loads, modifies the relevant registers and resets the GPU before handing control back to the unmodified driver. As a result, it does not require permanently flashing the card’s VBIOS or modified firmware. 
 In one community compatibility report , an RTX 3090 achieved 129.6 TFLOPS in BF16 matrix multiplication, up from 77.5 TFLOPS. TF32 performance increased from 40.2 to 69.8 TFLOPS. Its sibling, the RTX 3090 Ti , saw BF16 throughput jump from 87.5 to 157.4 TFLOPS. 
 That said, the gains are very workload-dependent. Another RTX 3090 user reported a 16% improvement in long-context prompt processing during local LLM inference, while token generation speeds remained practically unchanged. Separately, ComfyUI testing on an RTX 3090 Ti demonstrated roughly 47–59% higher throughput across several BF16-heavy image-generation workloads. 
 But what about gaming? Nvidia’s DLSS technology also uses Tensor Cores, raising the possibility that certain AI-assisted rendering operations could benefit. Unfortunately, no independently verified gaming benchmarks have established any FPS improvements. For now, the original project is limited to Linux, although a separate experimental Windows port has demonstrated an unlocked RTX 3090 successfully booting into Windows on one specific system. 
 The unlock also remains experimental, so installing it on a primary gaming PC carries risks. Nevertheless, the possibility of extracting substantially more computing performance from ageing RTX 30-series hardware without purchasing a new GPU is intriguing if you’re feeling adventurous.
